lines.source: old lab film, scene 1, first line: an answer that arrives after the moment it was needed
lines.text: A robot arm asks its AI where to reach. The answer comes back correct, and too late.

lines.source: the film's thesis, the author's own: the planner advises, the controller owns the timing
lines.text: Dr. Ozgur Ural's proposal fits in one line. Let the AI advise. Never let it hold the clock.

lines.source: old lab film, scene 1: at sixty hertz the controller gets 16.67 ms, every time
lines.text: A machine that moves runs on a beat. Many times a second, its controller must act. Not usually. Every time.

lines.source: old lab film, scene 1: inference time is variable; DeadlineModel's slow request takes several controller ticks
lines.text: Large AI models keep a different clock. Most answers are quick. A few take far longer, and no one knows in advance which.

lines.source: old lab film, scene 2: blocking inference delays later jobs too, red squares count missed deadlines
lines.text: Make the controller wait for the AI, and one slow answer costs it a beat. Then another. The arm freezes mid-task.

lines.source: old lab film, scene 2: a separate worker proposes updates and the controller never waits for it
lines.text: So the AI moves out of the waiting path. The controller keeps its beat no matter what. The AI works beside it and leaves its latest plan.

lines.source: old lab film, scene 3: the loop may stay on time while using an answer about a world that has changed
lines.text: Now nothing is late. But a plan can describe a world that has already moved.

lines.source: old lab film, scene 3: observation timestamp checked before use, fallback when a proposal expires
lines.text: So every plan is stamped with the moment it was made. Too old, and the controller sets it aside and does something safe.

lines.source: old lab film, scene 3: freshness is only one check; validate action limits separately. Pattern after the Simplex architecture (Sha, IEEE Software 2001)
lines.text: Even a fresh plan can be wrong. So a simple guard checks every command against hard limits, whatever the AI says.

lines.source: old lab film, scene 4 and DeadlineModel: async misses are zero when isolated and appear only under shared stalls
lines.text: One trap is left. If the AI and the controller share one chip, a busy AI can still steal the controller's time. Give each its own, and test under load.

lines.source: Simplex (Sha 2001) guards a complex controller with a simple verified one; the open part is large models with variable inference time and shared accelerators
lines.text: Safety engineers already guard complex controllers this way. The open question is doing it for today's large models, and proving the timing holds.

lines.source: the thesis, in the same words
lines.text: Smarter AI will keep arriving. Let the AI advise. Never let it hold the clock.
